title: The Missing Middle: What Mezzanine Finance Actually Solves Before You Give Away Equity
excerpt: When the bank won't lend enough and selling a stake feels too permanent, most Australian SME owners assume those are the only two options. There is usually a third, and almost nobody mentions it.
content:
A growing business asks its bank for more debt to fund an acquisition, a new site, or a step up in working capital. The bank comes back with a number well short of the request, capped by serviceability and the security available, not by the strength of the growth plan. The conversation that follows almost always jumps straight to the other extreme: bring in an investor, sell a slice of the business, raise the rest as equity.

That jump happens because most owners only ever hear about the two ends of the spectrum. Banks offer senior secured debt within their lending limits, and that is the full extent of what they are structured to offer. Advisers who specialise in equity raises are, understandably, inclined to talk about equity raises. Almost nobody in the room has a reason to mention the option that sits between the two, which is a shame, because for a specific kind of growth story it is often the better fit.

What sits between a term loan and selling a stake

Mezzanine finance is debt that sits behind a bank's senior facility in priority, which is what makes it riskier for the lender and more expensive than a standard business loan. In exchange for that risk, a mezzanine lender charges a higher interest rate and sometimes attaches a small equity kicker, an option or warrant over a modest slice of future value, rather than taking an ownership stake upfront. It behaves like debt. It gets repaid on a schedule, over a defined term, and then it is gone. It does not sit on the register forever the way an equity investor does.

Why it fits a specific kind of growth story, not every one

Mezzanine finance earns its cost when the capital is funding something specific and provable, an acquisition with a clear payback, a new location backed by demand you can already see, a contract that is signed but needs capital to deliver against. The business needs to be generating enough cash to service a higher interest cost for a defined window, because mezzanine is not patient capital in the way equity can be. If the growth plan is closer to an open-ended bet, a new market with no track record yet, a product still finding its customer, that uncertainty is exactly what equity investors are structured to absorb and mezzanine lenders are not.

What it actually costs, and what it protects

The honest cost comparison matters here. Mezzanine finance costs more in interest than a standard bank facility, sometimes considerably more, and that cost needs to be weighed against what it protects, which is full ownership and full control of every decision for the length of the arrangement. An equity raise permanently changes who sits around the table. A mezzanine facility, however expensive it feels in the moment, has an end date. For an owner who intends to still be running the business, and owning all of it, in five years, that difference is often worth more than the interest rate suggests on paper.

Why this conversation rarely happens on its own

The reason most owners never hear about this option isn't that it's hidden. It's that nobody they're already talking to is set up to recommend it. A bank will tell you what it can lend. An equity investor will tell you what a stake is worth. Working out whether debt, mezzanine or equity actually fits the shape of your growth need, before you start talking to either, is a structured piece of analysis most businesses skip because nobody raised it as a live option. That gap is exactly what a capital raise feasibility assessment is built to close, matching the instrument to the need rather than defaulting to whichever conversation started first.

None of this is a case against equity. Plenty of growth stories genuinely need a partner who shares the risk, not just a lender who wants repaying regardless of how the plan unfolds, and the investor readiness work that precedes a good equity raise is just as real. The point is narrower than that. Before assuming the choice is binary, it is worth finding out whether a structure exists that gets you the capital without permanently changing who owns the business. For businesses already running a live transaction, this is also where a fractional CFO capital markets engagement tends to earn its keep, managing the lender and investor conversations in parallel rather than one closing off the other by default.

faqs.q: What is mezzanine finance and how is it different from a bank loan?
faqs.a: It is debt that sits behind a bank's senior facility in priority, which makes it riskier for the lender and more expensive to borrow. In return, it typically comes with fewer security requirements than senior debt and sometimes a small equity kicker, but it still behaves like debt: it is repaid on a schedule over a defined term, not held indefinitely.

faqs.q: Is mezzanine finance more expensive than a standard business loan in Australia?
faqs.a: Yes, typically. The interest rate reflects the extra risk the lender is taking by sitting behind the bank's senior facility. Whether that cost is worth paying depends on what the capital is funding and how much control the alternative, usually equity, would cost you instead over the life of the business, not just over the term of the loan.

faqs.q: Does mezzanine finance mean giving up equity in my business?
faqs.a: Not in the way an equity raise does. Some mezzanine arrangements include a small equity kicker, an option over a modest slice of future value, but ownership and day to day control stay with the owner for the term of the facility. That is the main difference from selling a stake outright.

faqs.q: What kind of business qualifies for mezzanine finance over equity?
faqs.a: Businesses with a specific, provable use for the capital and cash generation strong enough to service a higher interest cost for a defined period tend to fit best, an acquisition, a new site, or a signed contract needing delivery capital. Open-ended growth bets with no track record are usually a better fit for equity.

faqs.q: How long does a mezzanine finance arrangement usually run for?
faqs.a: It is structured as a defined term, commonly a small number of years, rather than an open-ended arrangement. That fixed horizon is part of its appeal against equity, which has no natural end date once a stake has been sold, and it gives the owner a clear point at which the business is fully theirs again.

faqs.q: When should an SME consider mezzanine finance instead of raising equity?
faqs.a: When the business can already demonstrate strong, provable cash flow and the growth need is specific rather than speculative, mezzanine is worth assessing before defaulting to an equity conversation. A proper capital raise feasibility review compares all three instruments against the actual need rather than whichever option was raised first.

faqs.q: Can a fractional CFO help structure a mezzanine finance deal?
faqs.a: Yes. Structuring and negotiating a mezzanine facility alongside existing bank arrangements is exactly the kind of transaction work a capital markets engagement is designed for, managing lender terms, modelling the repayment impact on the business, and keeping the conversation separate from any parallel equity discussion that might also be underway.
